segments.text: International disputes may be settled through diplomatic or adjudicative methods rather than force.
Diplomatic methods keep greater control with the parties; adjudicative methods such as arbitration and judicial settlement produce legal decisions based on consent to jurisdiction.

The UN Charter requires members to settle international disputes by peaceful means so that international peace, security and justice are not endangered. Peaceful settlement is a family of methods rather than one procedure. The choice depends on consent, urgency, political relations, subject matter and whether the parties want a negotiated or legally binding outcome.

Negotiation is direct engagement between the parties. Good offices involve a third party helping the parties come together. Mediation involves more active assistance in developing a settlement. Inquiry clarifies disputed facts. Conciliation generally combines investigation with non-binding proposals.

Arbitration is adjudication based on consent in which the parties submit a dispute to a tribunal and receive an award. The parties often have greater control over composition and procedure than in a permanent court. Judicial settlement before the ICJ is also consent-based in contentious cases, but the Court is a permanent judicial institution operating under its Statute and Rules.

Consent to ICJ jurisdiction can arise through a compromissory clause in a treaty, a special agreement, reciprocal optional-clause declarations, or another valid jurisdictional basis. The Court cannot simply hear every dispute between UN member states.

Comparison should focus on four variables: how much control the parties retain, what the third party does, whether the result is legally binding, and whether the process applies law or seeks a negotiated compromise. Diplomatic methods may preserve relationships and flexibility; adjudication can provide authoritative legal resolution but requires a jurisdictional basis.

items.text: Begin by separating diplomatic methods from adjudicative methods. Diplomatic methods aim at negotiated settlement and leave more control with the parties; adjudicative methods apply law to produce a legal decision.

Negotiation is direct communication. Good offices help bring parties together; mediation involves more active third-party participation; inquiry clarifies disputed facts; conciliation may investigate and propose settlement terms.

Arbitration depends on consent to submit a dispute to a tribunal chosen or constituted for that dispute or category of disputes. Judicial settlement before the ICJ also depends on a valid basis of consent to jurisdiction.
In an exam comparison, always mention the third party's role, whether the result is binding, the degree of party control, and whether the process is legal or primarily diplomatic.

rows: Common confusion to avoid: Do not assume the ICJ can hear every international dispute automatically. Contentious jurisdiction is based on state consent.
